notes:
1. India as a Union of States

  • Article 1 declares that India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.

The Constitution therefore recognises two constitutional names:

  • India.
  • Bharat.
  • Both names are constitutionally valid.
  • The expression used is “Union of States,” not “Federation of States.”
  • Article 1 establishes the territorial and constitutional identity of India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 1 → India, that is Bharat → Union of States

2. Why “Union” and Not “Federation”?

  • The Constituent Assembly deliberately used the expression “Union of States.”
  • The Indian Union was not created through an agreement among previously sovereign States.
  • States do not possess a constitutional right to secede from India.
  • The Union is intended to be permanent.
  • Parliament possesses constitutional authority to reorganise State territories and boundaries.
  • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar explained that the federation was not the result of an agreement among States and that no State had a right to separate from India.
  • This idea is commonly expressed as an indestructible Union of destructible States.
  • That expression is explanatory and does not appear verbatim in Article 1.
📌 Must-Memorise

Union → Permanent
State Boundaries → Alterable

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

“Indestructible Union of Destructible States” → Explanatory Phrase
Not Exact Constitutional Wording

3. Union and Union Government

  • The word “Union” may be used in two related but different senses.
  • Union as a political community refers to India as one constitutional territorial entity.
  • Union Government refers to governmental institutions operating at the national level.
  • These meanings should not be confused.
  • Article 1 primarily concerns India's constitutional territorial identity.

4. Federal Significance of Article 1

  • Article 1 establishes India's territorial unity.
  • It does not itself contain the detailed distribution of powers between the Union and States.

The federal distribution of powers is dealt with primarily through:

  • Seventh Schedule.
  • Part XI.
  • Other federal provisions.
  • Detailed federalism belongs to Chapter 17.

5. Article 1(1) — Constitutional Name

  • Article 1(1) provides that India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.
  • “India” and “Bharat” are therefore constitutionally recognised names.
  • The phrase “shall be” expresses the continuing constitutional character of India as a Union of States.
  • It is not merely a description of the political situation that existed in 1950.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 1(1) → India + Bharat

6. Article 1(2) — States and Their Territories

  • Article 1(2) provides that the States and their territories shall be as specified in the First Schedule.
  • The First Schedule therefore has direct constitutional importance in determining the territorial composition of India.
  • Changes in State boundaries, areas or names may require corresponding alterations in the First Schedule.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 1(2) → States and Territories → First Schedule

7. Article 1(3) — Territory of India

The territory of India comprises:

  • Territories of the States.
  • Union Territories specified in the First Schedule.
  • Territories that may be acquired by India.
  • These three categories constitute the constitutional territory of India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Territory of India = States + Union Territories + Acquired Territories

8. Union of India vs Territory of India

  • The Union of India generally refers to the federal political unit consisting primarily of the States participating in the constitutional federal structure.
  • The territory of India is wider.

It includes:

  • Territories of States.
  • Union Territories.
  • Territories acquired by India.
  • A Union Territory forms part of the territory of India even though it is not constitutionally identical to a State.
  • An acquired territory may become part of the territory of India before Parliament determines its final administrative status.
⭐ TNPSC Favourite

Every State → Part of Territory of India
Territory of India → Not Confined to States

9. First Schedule

The First Schedule specifies:

  • Names of States.
  • Territories of States.
  • Names of Union Territories.
  • Territorial descriptions of Union Territories.
  • It is directly connected with Articles 1 and 4.
  • State-reorganisation laws may require corresponding amendments to the First Schedule.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Schedule → States + UTs + Territorial Descriptions

10. First Schedule vs Fourth Schedule

  • The First Schedule deals with States, Union Territories and their territorial descriptions.
  • The Fourth Schedule deals with allocation of seats in the Rajya Sabha.
  • Territorial reorganisation can affect both territory and parliamentary representation.
  • A reorganisation law may therefore require changes to both Schedules.
📌 Must-Memorise

First Schedule → Territory
Fourth Schedule → Rajya Sabha Seats

11. Article 2 — Admission or Establishment of New States

  • Article 2 authorises Parliament to admit into the Union new States.
  • It also authorises Parliament to establish new States.
  • Parliament may do so on such terms and conditions as it considers appropriate.
  • The power belongs to Parliament.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 2 → Admission or Establishment of New States

12. Scope of Article 2

  • Article 2 mainly concerns territories not already forming part of the existing Indian Union.

It may apply where:

  • A foreign territory joins India.
  • Newly acquired territory is established as a State.
  • A political entity outside the existing Union is admitted.
  • Admission generally suggests incorporation of an already existing political entity.
  • Establishment may involve creation of a new State from territory not previously organised as a State of the Indian Union.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Article 2 → External Addition to Existing Union

13. Terms and Conditions under Article 2

Parliament may prescribe terms and conditions relating to:

  • Administration.
  • Representation.
  • Institutional transition.
  • Legal continuity.
  • Territorial arrangements.
  • Such conditions remain subject to the Constitution.

14. Article 2 vs Article 3

  • Article 2 primarily concerns admission or establishment of a new State involving territory outside the existing Union.
  • Article 3 principally concerns internal territorial reorganisation.
  • Article 3 deals with existing States and territories within India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 2 → Admit/Establish
Article 3 → Internal Reorganisation

15. Article 3 — Five Main Powers of Parliament

Under Article 3, Parliament may:

  • Form a new State.
  • Increase the area of a State.
  • Diminish the area of a State.
  • Alter the boundaries of a State.
  • Alter the name of a State.
🧠 Ultra-Short Memory

Form → Increase → Diminish → Boundary → Name

16. Formation of a New State under Article 3

Parliament may form a new State by:

  • Separating territory from an existing State.
  • Uniting two or more States.
  • Uniting parts of two or more States.
  • Uniting any territory with a part of a State.
  • Article 3 therefore gives Parliament extensive flexibility in territorial reorganisation.

17. Increase or Diminution of State Area

  • Parliament may increase the area of an existing State.
  • Parliament may diminish the area of an existing State.
  • Territory may therefore be added to or removed from a State through constitutional legislation under Article 3.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 3 → Increase or Diminish State Area

18. Alteration of State Boundaries

  • Parliament may alter the territorial boundaries of a State.
  • Internal State boundaries are therefore not constitutionally permanent.
  • An alteration of internal State boundaries does not by itself require the Article 368 constitutional-amendment procedure.

19. Alteration of State Name

  • Parliament may alter the name of an existing State under Article 3.
  • A State may request a name change.
  • However, Parliament's constitutional authority does not depend on the State initiating the proposal.
  • The constitutionally prescribed consultation procedure must nevertheless be followed.
📌 Must-Memorise

Change of State Name → Article 3

20. Width of Parliament's Power under Article 3

  • Article 3 gives Parliament extensive power over the territorial organisation of States.

A State cannot constitutionally veto Parliament from:

  • Dividing it.
  • Combining it with another State.
  • Changing its area.
  • Altering its boundary.
  • Changing its name.
  • However, the Constitution requires consultation with the affected State Legislature in specified cases.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

State Reorganisation → Parliament Has Final Legislative Authority

21. President's Recommendation for Article 3 Bill

  • A Bill under Article 3 may be introduced in Parliament only with the prior recommendation of the President.
  • It cannot be introduced as an ordinary private member's Bill without such recommendation.
  • Presidential recommendation is therefore a constitutional prerequisite.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 3 Bill → Prior Recommendation of President

22. Reference to the Affected State Legislature

  • Where a proposal affects the area, boundary or name of a State, the President must refer the Bill to the Legislature of that State.
  • The State Legislature is given an opportunity to express its views.
  • The President specifies the period within which those views should be communicated.
  • The President may extend the period.
📌 Must-Memorise

President → Refers Bill → State Legislature → Views

23. Role of the State Legislature

The affected State Legislature may:

  • Approve the proposal.
  • Oppose the proposal.
  • Suggest modifications.
  • Fail to communicate its views within the specified period.
  • The Constitution requires consultation with the State Legislature.
  • It does not require the State Legislature's consent.
⭐ TNPSC Favourite

State Legislature → Views Required
Consent → Not Required

24. If the State Legislature Opposes

  • Parliament may still enact the reorganisation law even if the affected State Legislature opposes the proposal.
  • The State Legislature's opinion is not binding on Parliament.
  • Article 3 therefore gives the State a consultative role rather than a constitutional veto.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

State Opposition ≠ Bar on Parliament

25. If the State Legislature Does Not Respond

  • The State Legislature is given a specified period to express its views.
  • The President may extend that period.
  • If the prescribed period expires without a response, Parliament may proceed with the proposal.

26. Why the State Is Consulted

The consultation process allows the State to place on record concerns relating to:

  • Administration.
  • Language.
  • Regional identity.
  • Resources.
  • Public opinion.
  • Territorial interests.
  • Consultation gives the State a constitutional voice without transferring final authority from Parliament.

27. State Legislature in a Bicameral State

  • Where a State has two Houses, the constitutional expression “Legislature of the State” refers to the State Legislature as constitutionally constituted.
  • It does not simply mean the Legislative Assembly alone.

28. Parliament May Modify the Article 3 Bill

  • Parliament is not constitutionally required to retain the proposal in exactly the form referred to the State Legislature.
  • Parliament may modify the proposal during the legislative process.
  • A fresh reference to the State Legislature is not generally required merely because details of the proposal are subsequently changed.
📌 TNPSC Key Point

Initial State Consultation → Required
Every Parliamentary Modification → Fresh Reference Not Normally Required

29. State Initiative Is Not Essential

  • A State Legislature may pass a resolution requesting reorganisation or a change of name.
  • However, Article 3 does not require the State to initiate the process.
  • Parliament's constitutional power exists independently of such a State resolution.

30. “State” and Union Territory under Article 3

  • For specified purposes under Article 3, the expression “State” includes a Union Territory.
  • This allows Article 3 to operate in relation to territorial arrangements involving Union Territories.
  • However, this inclusion does not operate identically in every procedural context.
  • For the proviso requiring reference to a State Legislature, “State” does not include a Union Territory.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 3 Main Clauses → State Includes UT
Article 3 Proviso → State Does Not Include UT

31. Article 4 — Supplemental and Consequential Provisions

  • A law made under Article 2 or Article 3 may include provisions necessary to give effect to territorial change.

Article 4 permits:

  • Supplemental provisions.
  • Incidental provisions.
  • Consequential provisions.
  • This enables Parliament to deal with the practical consequences of State reorganisation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 4 → Supplemental + Incidental + Consequential Provisions

32. Matters That May Be Covered under Article 4

A reorganisation law may contain provisions relating to:

  • First Schedule.
  • Fourth Schedule.
  • Parliamentary representation.
  • State legislative representation.
  • Distribution of assets and liabilities.
  • Continuity of laws.
  • Public services.
  • Courts and legal proceedings.
  • Administrative transition.
  • Other necessary consequential matters.

33. Representation after Reorganisation

Territorial change may affect representation in:

  • Lok Sabha.
  • Rajya Sabha.
  • State Legislative Assemblies.
  • State Legislative Councils where applicable.
  • Article 4 permits consequential legislative adjustments to these arrangements.

34. Administrative Continuity after Reorganisation

  • Reorganisation legislation may determine which existing laws continue to apply.
  • It may allocate officers and public services.
  • It may divide institutions.
  • It may distribute assets and liabilities.
  • It may determine which government assumes existing obligations.
  • These provisions prevent a legal or administrative vacuum.

35. Simple Majority under Articles 2–4

  • A law under Articles 2 or 3 is enacted through the ordinary parliamentary legislative procedure.
  • It is commonly described for examination purposes as requiring a simple majority.
  • The required majority is a majority of members present and voting.
  • Ratification by half of the States is not required for ordinary reorganisation legislation under Articles 2–4.
📌 Must-Memorise

Articles 2–4 → Simple Majority
State Ratification → Not Required

36. Article 4 vs Article 368

  • Article 4(2) provides that a law under Articles 2 or 3 is not deemed to be a constitutional amendment for the purposes of Article 368.
  • This remains true even when the law alters the First or Fourth Schedule.
  • The Constitution itself authorises such consequential changes through ordinary legislation.
⭐ TNPSC Favourite

Change in First Schedule ≠ Always Article 368 Amendment

37. Internal Reorganisation vs Foreign Cession

Internal reorganisation:

  • Articles 3 and 4.
  • Ordinary parliamentary law.
  • Simple majority.
  • No binding State consent.

Cession of Indian territory to a foreign State:

  • Cannot be completed merely under Article 3.
  • Requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
📌 Must-Memorise

Internal Reorganisation → Article 3
Foreign Cession → Article 368

38. Acquisition of Foreign Territory

  • Article 1(3)(c) recognises territories that may be acquired by India.

As a sovereign State, India may acquire territory through legally recognised processes such as:

  • Treaty.
  • Agreement.
  • Purchase.
  • Cession by another country.
  • Accession.
  • Other recognised international processes.
  • Acquisition gives India sovereignty over the territory.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 1(3)(c) → Acquired Territories

39. Administration of Acquired Territory

After acquisition, Parliament may determine whether the territory should be:

  • Merged with an existing State.
  • Constituted as a Union Territory.
  • Established as a new State.
  • Administered through a transitional arrangement.
  • Acquisition and internal constitutional organisation are conceptually distinct stages.

40. Acquisition vs Admission

  • Acquisition refers to India obtaining sovereignty over territory.
  • Admission or establishment concerns the constitutional manner in which that territory is incorporated into India's internal political structure.
  • Acquisition does not automatically determine whether the territory will become a State or Union Territory.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Acquisition ≠ Automatic Statehood

41. Historical Examples of Territorial Integration

Territories integrated into India after commencement of the Constitution included:

  • Chandernagore.
  • Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
  • Goa, Daman and Diu.
  • Puducherry and associated former French establishments.
  • Sikkim through a distinct constitutional process.

42. Cession of Indian Territory

  • Cession means transfer of Indian territory to another country.
  • Article 3 deals principally with internal territorial reorganisation.
  • It does not by itself authorise transfer of Indian territory to a foreign State.
  • The constitutional position was examined by the Supreme Court in the Berubari Union Reference.

43. Berubari Union Reference, 1960

  • The Berubari Union Reference arose from proposed territorial arrangements involving India and Pakistan.
  • The Supreme Court held that cession of Indian territory to a foreign State requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
  • A law under Article 3 alone is insufficient.
  • The case also expressed the then-prevailing view that the Preamble was not part of the Constitution.
  • That Preamble proposition was later displaced by Kesavananda Bharati, 1973.
  • The territorial-cession principle remains important.
📌 Must-Memorise

Berubari Union → 1960
Foreign Cession → Constitutional Amendment Required

44. Ninth Constitutional Amendment, 1960

  • The Constitution (Ninth Amendment) Act, 1960 facilitated implementation of territorial arrangements connected with India and Pakistan.
  • It was associated with the Berubari Union and related boundary exchanges.
📌 Must-Memorise

9th Amendment, 1960 → Berubari-related Territorial Arrangement

45. Boundary Demarcation vs Cession

  • Not every settlement of an international boundary amounts to cession of Indian territory.
  • Boundary demarcation identifies the correct boundary where its location is uncertain or disputed.
  • Cession transfers territory already recognised as belonging to India.
  • The constitutional consequences depend on whether the arrangement is a boundary settlement or an actual transfer of territory.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Boundary Settlement ≠ Necessarily Territorial Cession

46. Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel Case, 1969

Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India, 1969 distinguished between:

  • Cession of Indian territory.
  • Settlement or demarcation of a disputed boundary.
  • A constitutional amendment may not be necessary when an agreement merely identifies the true boundary rather than transferring recognised Indian territory.
📌 Must-Memorise

Maganbhai Patel → Boundary Settlement vs Cession

47. One Hundredth Constitutional Amendment, 2015

  • The Constitution (One Hundredth Amendment) Act, 2015 implemented territorial arrangements under the India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement.

It gave effect to:

  • Exchange of enclaves.
  • Settlement of adverse possessions.
  • Final boundary arrangements.
  • The First Schedule was modified accordingly.
📌 Must-Memorise

100th Amendment, 2015 → India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement

48. Territorial Position at Independence

At independence, the Indian subcontinent included:

  • Former British Indian provinces.
  • Princely States.
  • Chief Commissioners' Provinces.
  • Territories under French control.
  • Territories under Portuguese control.
  • Integration of these varied territories was essential for formation of the modern Indian Union.

49. Integration of Princely States

  • Princely States were not administered in the same manner as British Indian provinces.

Their integration involved:

  • Instruments of Accession.
  • Merger agreements.
  • Political negotiations.
  • Administrative consolidation.
  • Their integration was one of the major nation-building tasks after independence.

50. Role of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V.P. Menon

  • Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, as Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, played a leading political role in integration of princely States.
  • V.P. Menon played an important administrative and negotiating role.
  • Their efforts helped consolidate numerous princely States into the Indian Union.
📌 Must-Memorise

Integration of Princely States → Sardar Patel + V.P. Menon

51. Constitutional Classification in 1950

The original First Schedule classified territorial units into four broad categories:

  • Part A States.
  • Part B States.
  • Part C States.
  • Part D territory.
  • This classification was substantially changed in 1956.

52. Part A, Part B, Part C and Part D

  • Part A States consisted mainly of former Governors' Provinces.
  • Part B States consisted mainly of former princely States or unions of princely States.
  • Part C States consisted largely of former Chief Commissioners' Provinces and certain princely territories.
  • Part D consisted of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
📌 Must-Memorise

Part A → Governors' Provinces
Part B → Princely States/Unions
Part C → Chief Commissioners' Provinces + Certain Princely Territories
Part D → Andaman and Nicobar Islands

53. Abolition of Part A–D Classification

  • The Part A, B, C and D classification was removed during the territorial reorganisation of 1956.

The constitutional framework thereafter distinguished primarily between:

  • States.
  • Union Territories.
  • The Seventh Constitutional Amendment was central to this restructuring.
📌 Must-Memorise

1956 → Part A/B/C/D Classification Removed

54. Demand for Linguistic States

  • Language emerged as a major basis for territorial reorganisation after independence.

Supporters of linguistic States argued that such States could improve:

  • Administration.
  • Democratic participation.
  • Education.
  • Cultural recognition.
  • The Union government initially approached immediate linguistic reorganisation cautiously.

55. Dhar Commission, 1948

  • The Linguistic Provinces Commission was appointed in 1948.
  • It was headed by S.K. Dhar.
  • It did not recommend immediate reorganisation purely on linguistic lines.

It emphasised factors such as:

  • Administrative convenience.
  • National unity.
  • Economic viability.
📌 Must-Memorise

Dhar Commission → 1948 → S.K. Dhar

56. JVP Committee

The JVP Committee consisted of:

  • Jawaharlal Nehru.
  • Vallabhbhai Patel.
  • Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
  • The name JVP comes from the initials of these three leaders.
  • The Committee generally advised postponement of linguistic reorganisation.
  • It recognised that strong public demands could require reconsideration.
📌 Must-Memorise

JVP → Jawaharlal Nehru + Vallabhbhai Patel + Pattabhi Sitaramayya

57. Andhra State, 1953

  • Potti Sriramulu's death following a fast intensified the demand for a Telugu-speaking State.
  • Andhra State was created in 1953.
  • It was the first State created primarily on a linguistic basis after independence.
  • Its creation accelerated demands for wider linguistic reorganisation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Andhra State → 1953
Potti Sriramulu → Linguistic State Movement

58. States Reorganisation Commission, 1953

  • The States Reorganisation Commission was appointed in 1953.
  • Fazl Ali was Chairman.
  • K.M. Panikkar was a member.
  • H.N. Kunzru was a member.

The Commission considered:

  • Language.
  • Administrative convenience.
  • Economic viability.
  • National unity.
  • Communication.
  • Regional interests.
📌 Must-Memorise

SRC → 1953
Chairman → Fazl Ali
Members → K.M. Panikkar + H.N. Kunzru

59. States Reorganisation Act, 1956

  • The States Reorganisation Act, 1956 substantially reorganised India's internal boundaries.
  • Language was an important consideration.
  • Administrative and economic factors were also taken into account.
  • The Act became a major foundation of India's modern territorial map.
  • The reorganisation took effect on 1 November 1956.
📌 Must-Memorise

States Reorganisation Act → 1956
Effective → 1 November 1956

60. Seventh Constitutional Amendment, 1956

  • The Seventh Constitutional Amendment supported the territorial reorganisation of 1956.
  • It removed the old Part A, B, C and D classification.
  • It revised the constitutional framework for States and Union Territories.
  • It made consequential constitutional changes required by the new territorial structure.
📌 Must-Memorise

7th Amendment, 1956 → States + Union Territories Framework

61. Territorial Position after 1956 Reorganisation

From 1 November 1956, India was reorganised into:

  • 14 States.
  • 6 Union Territories.
  • This arrangement became an important foundation for later territorial changes.
📌 Must-Memorise

1956 → 14 States + 6 Union Territories

62. Bombay Reorganisation, 1960

  • The bilingual Bombay State was divided in 1960.

Two States emerged:

  • Maharashtra.
  • Gujarat.
  • Linguistic considerations played an important role.
📌 Must-Memorise

1960 → Maharashtra + Gujarat

63. Goa, Daman and Diu

  • Former Portuguese territories were incorporated into India in the early 1960s.
  • Goa, Daman and Diu were constituted as a Union Territory.
  • Goa later became a State in 1987.
  • Daman and Diu continued as a Union Territory until later administrative reorganisation.

64. Nagaland and Punjab Reorganisation

  • Nagaland became a State in 1963.
  • Punjab was reorganised in 1966.

The reorganisation resulted in:

  • Punjab.
  • Haryana.
  • Union Territory of Chandigarh.
  • Certain territories were also transferred to Himachal Pradesh.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nagaland → 1963
Haryana → 1966
Chandigarh → Union Territory

65. Himachal Pradesh and North-Eastern Statehood

  • Himachal Pradesh became a State in 1971.

In 1972, Statehood was granted to:

  • Manipur.
  • Tripura.
  • Meghalaya.
  • Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh initially continued under Union Territory arrangements before later Statehood.
📌 Must-Memorise

Himachal Pradesh → 1971
Manipur + Tripura + Meghalaya → 1972

66. Sikkim

  • Sikkim entered the Indian constitutional framework through a distinct process.
  • The Thirty-Fifth Constitutional Amendment provided an associate-status arrangement.
  • The Thirty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment, 1975 made Sikkim a full State of India.
  • Article 371F provides special constitutional provisions relating to Sikkim.
📌 Must-Memorise

35th Amendment → Sikkim Associate Arrangement
36th Amendment → Sikkim Full State → 1975

67. Statehood in 1987

In 1987, Statehood was granted to:

  • Mizoram.
  • Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Goa.
📌 Must-Memorise

1987 → Mizoram + Arunachal Pradesh + Goa

68. Three New States in 2000

Three States were created in 2000:

  • Chhattisgarh from Madhya Pradesh.
  • Uttaranchal from Uttar Pradesh.
  • Jharkhand from Bihar.
  • Uttaranchal was later renamed Uttarakhand.
📌 Must-Memorise

2000 → Chhattisgarh + Uttarakhand + Jharkhand

69. Telangana, 2014

  • Telangana was formed in 2014.
  • It was created from the existing State of Andhra Pradesh.
  • Its formation occurred through parliamentary reorganisation legislation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Telangana → 2014 → From Andhra Pradesh

70. Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation, 2019

  • The former State of Jammu and Kashmir was reorganised in 2019.

Two Union Territories were created:

  • Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Ladakh.
  • This reduced the total number of States and altered the Union Territory structure.
📌 Must-Memorise

2019 → Jammu and Kashmir UT + Ladakh UT

71. Merger of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu

  • The Union Territories of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu were merged.
  • The merged Union Territory came into existence in 2020.

Its name is:

  • Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
📌 Must-Memorise

2020 → Dadra and Nagar Haveli + Daman and Diu → One UT

72. Present Territorial Position

According to the reference material, India presently consists of:

  • 28 States.
  • 8 Union Territories.
  • The reference records the Government of India's national portal position updated on 28 July 2026.
📌 Must-Memorise

Present India → 28 States + 8 Union Territories

73. Eight Union Territories

The eight Union Territories are:

  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
  • Chandigarh.
  • Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
  • National Capital Territory of Delhi.
  • Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Ladakh.
  • Lakshadweep.
  • Puducherry.

74. Union Territories with Legislative Arrangements

  • Delhi has a Legislative Assembly under special constitutional provisions.
  • Puducherry has a Legislative Assembly.
  • Jammu and Kashmir has legislative provisions under its reorganisation framework.
  • Other Union Territories do not operate under the same legislative model.
  • Detailed Union Territory administration belongs to Chapter 6.

75. Administration of Union Territories

  • Union Territories are constitutionally administered by the President.
  • Administration is carried out through an Administrator or Lieutenant Governor appointed under the constitutional framework.
  • Articles 239 to 241 contain important provisions relating to Union Territories.
  • The Ministry of Home Affairs is the Union's nodal ministry for core Union Territory matters.

76. Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay, 1960

  • The case concerned constitutional procedure relating to State reorganisation.
  • The Supreme Court recognised the extensive power of Parliament under Article 3.
  • It affirmed the consultative nature of the State Legislature's role.
  • The State Legislature's views do not bind Parliament.
📌 Must-Memorise

Babulal Parate → State Views under Article 3 Not Binding

77. State of West Bengal v. Union of India, 1963

  • The Supreme Court rejected the view that Indian States possess sovereignty independent of the Union.
  • It emphasised that the Indian Constitution did not arise from a compact among sovereign States.
  • The case reinforces the constitutional understanding of India as a Union rather than a federation created by an agreement among sovereign States.
📌 Must-Memorise

State of West Bengal v. Union of India → States Not Separately Sovereign

78. Mangal Singh v. Union of India, 1967

  • The Supreme Court recognised the wide scope of Parliament's power under Articles 3 and 4.

Parliament may make:

  • Supplemental provisions.
  • Incidental provisions.
  • Consequential provisions.
  • These provisions may be necessary to make territorial reorganisation effective.
  • Article 4 cannot, however, be used to disregard unrelated constitutional limitations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Mangal Singh → Wide Incidental Powers under Article 4

79. Important Case Associations

  • In Re: Berubari Union, 1960 → Cession to foreign country requires constitutional amendment.
  • Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay, 1960 → State Legislature's views under Article 3 are not binding.
  • State of West Bengal v. Union of India, 1963 → States are not independently sovereign.
  • Mangal Singh v. Union of India, 1967 → Wide supplemental and consequential powers under Article 4.
  • Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India, 1969 → Boundary settlement distinguished from territorial cession.

80. Article Mapping

  • Article 1 → Name and territory of the Union.
  • Article 2 → Admission or establishment of new States.
  • Article 3 → Formation of new States and alteration of area, boundary or name.
  • Article 4 → Supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions.
📌 Must-Memorise

1 → Name & Territory
2 → Admit/Establish
3 → Form/Reorganise
4 → Consequential Provisions

81. TNPSC Traps

  • India and Bharat → Both constitutionally valid names.
  • Article 1 → Union of States.
  • “Federation of States” → Not wording used in Article 1.
  • States → No constitutional right to secede.
  • Territory of India → Wider than Union of States.
  • Territory of India → States + UTs + acquired territories.
  • First Schedule → States, UTs and territorial descriptions.
  • Fourth Schedule → Rajya Sabha seats.
  • Article 2 → Admission or establishment.
  • Article 3 → Internal reorganisation.
  • Article 3 → Form, increase, diminish, boundary, name.
  • Article 3 Bill → President's prior recommendation.
  • State Legislature → Views required.
  • State Legislature consent → Not required.
  • State's views → Not binding on Parliament.
  • Parliament → May modify proposal.
  • Fresh reference after every modification → Not generally required.
  • Article 3 clauses → State may include UT.
  • Article 3 proviso → State does not include UT.
  • Article 4 → Supplemental, incidental and consequential provisions.
  • Articles 2–4 → Simple majority.
  • Article 2/3 law → Not Article 368 amendment.
  • Acquisition → Article 1(3)(c).
  • Cession to foreign country → Article 368 amendment.
  • Berubari → Foreign cession.
  • Maganbhai → Boundary demarcation vs cession.
  • Dhar Commission → S.K. Dhar.
  • JVP → Nehru + Patel + Pattabhi Sitaramayya.
  • Andhra State → 1953.
  • SRC Chairman → Fazl Ali.
  • States Reorganisation Act → 1956.
  • 1956 → 14 States + 6 UTs.
  • Sikkim → 36th Amendment, 1975.
  • Telangana → 2014.
  • Jammu and Kashmir reorganisation → 2019.
  • Present → 28 States + 8 UTs.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

Which Part deals with the Union and its territory? → Part I.

Which Articles are in Part I? → Articles 1–4.

Which Article declares India a Union of States? → Article 1.

What are the two constitutional names? → India and Bharat.

Why did Ambedkar prefer “Union” to “Federation”? → India was not formed by an agreement among sovereign States and States have no right to secede.

Does any State possess a constitutional right to leave India? → No.

What is meant by the explanatory phrase “indestructible Union of destructible States”? → The Union is permanent while State boundaries and territorial arrangements may be altered.

Does that phrase appear verbatim in Article 1? → No.

What does Article 1(2) deal with? → States and their territories as specified in the First Schedule.

What does Article 1(3) include? → States, Union Territories and acquired territories.

Is the territory of India wider than the Union of States? → Yes.

Which Schedule lists States and Union Territories? → First Schedule.

Which Schedule allocates Rajya Sabha seats? → Fourth Schedule.

Which Article empowers Parliament to admit or establish new States? → Article 2.

Which Article principally deals with internal reorganisation? → Article 3.

What five powers does Article 3 give Parliament? → Form a State, increase area, diminish area, alter boundaries and alter name.

Can Parliament divide an existing State? → Yes.

Can Parliament combine States or parts of States? → Yes.

Can Parliament change a State's name? → Yes.

What is necessary before introduction of an Article 3 Bill? → Prior recommendation of the President.

What happens if the proposal affects a State's area, boundary or name? → The President refers it to the affected State Legislature for its views.

Is consent of the State Legislature required? → No.

Are the State Legislature's views binding? → No.

Can Parliament proceed if the State opposes the proposal? → Yes.

Can Parliament proceed if the State does not respond within the permitted period? → Yes.

May the President extend the consultation period? → Yes.

Can a State initiate a request for reorganisation? → Yes, but Parliament's constitutional power does not depend on State initiation.

Can Parliament modify the Bill after State consultation? → Yes.

Is fresh State reference generally mandatory after every modification? → No.

Under Article 3, can “State” include a Union Territory? → Yes, for specified purposes.

Does “State” include a Union Territory in the proviso requiring State-Legislature consultation? → No.

Which Article allows supplemental and consequential provisions? → Article 4.

What Schedules may be altered under Article 4? → First and Fourth Schedules.

Can reorganisation law deal with assets and liabilities? → Yes.

Can it deal with public services and continuity of laws? → Yes.

Can it alter representation in Parliament and State Legislatures? → Yes.

What majority is required for ordinary legislation under Articles 2–4? → Simple majority.

Does an Article 3 reorganisation normally require Article 368? → No.

Does changing the First Schedule always mean a formal constitutional amendment? → No.

Which Article recognises acquired territories? → Article 1(3)(c).

What is acquisition? → India obtaining sovereignty over territory.

Does acquired territory automatically become a State? → No.

What is cession? → Transfer of Indian territory to another country.

Which case held that foreign cession requires constitutional amendment? → In Re: Berubari Union, 1960.

Which Amendment was associated with the Berubari territorial arrangement? → Ninth Constitutional Amendment, 1960.

Which case distinguished boundary settlement from cession? → Maganbhai Ishwarbhai Patel v. Union of India, 1969.

Which Amendment implemented the India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement? → 100th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2015.

Who played the leading political role in integration of princely States? → Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

Who played an important administrative and negotiating role? → V.P. Menon.

What were the original territorial classes in 1950? → Part A, Part B, Part C and Part D.

What were Part A States mainly? → Former Governors' Provinces.

What were Part B States mainly? → Former princely States or unions of princely States.

What were Part C States mainly? → Chief Commissioners' Provinces and certain princely territories.

What was Part D? → Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

When was the A/B/C/D classification abolished? → 1956.

Who headed the Dhar Commission? → S.K. Dhar.

When was the Dhar Commission appointed? → 1948.

Who were members of the JVP Committee? → Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya.

Which State was created in 1953 primarily on linguistic grounds? → Andhra State.

Whose fast and death intensified the Andhra movement? → Potti Sriramulu.

When was the States Reorganisation Commission appointed? → 1953.

Who chaired it? → Fazl Ali.

Who were its other members? → K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru.

Which major law reorganised States in 1956? → States Reorganisation Act, 1956.

Which constitutional amendment supported it? → Seventh Constitutional Amendment, 1956.

When did the reorganisation take effect? → 1 November 1956.

How many States and UTs existed after the 1956 reorganisation? → 14 States and 6 Union Territories.

Which States emerged from Bombay State in 1960? → Maharashtra and Gujarat.

When did Nagaland become a State? → 1963.

Which State was created in the 1966 Punjab reorganisation? → Haryana.

Which Union Territory emerged in that reorganisation? → Chandigarh.

When did Himachal Pradesh become a State? → 1971.

Which three States obtained Statehood in 1972? → Manipur, Tripura and Meghalaya.

Which Amendment made Sikkim a full State? → 36th Amendment, 1975.

Which States obtained Statehood in 1987? → Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa.

Which three States were created in 2000? → Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand and Jharkhand.

When was Telangana created? → 2014.

What happened to the former State of Jammu and Kashmir in 2019? → It was reorganised into the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.

Which two Union Territories were merged in 2020? → Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.

How many States and Union Territories does the reference record at present? → 28 States and 8 Union Territories.

Which case held that State views under Article 3 are consultative? → Babulal Parate v. State of Bombay, 1960.

Which case held that States are not independently sovereign? → State of West Bengal v. Union of India, 1963.

Which case recognised wide supplemental powers under Articles 3 and 4? → Mangal Singh v. Union of India, 1967.
